strengths: The paper addresses a significant problem: obtaining dense rewards for visual robotic reinforcement learning from action-free videos. Learning normalized temporal distance between frame pairs is simple, computationally attractive, and potentially useful.

The experimental evaluation is substantial within Meta-World: ten manipulation tasks, eight random seeds, comparisons with several progress-based and imitation-from-observation methods, and privileged BC and hand-designed dense-reward references. TimeRewarder achieves strong downstream performance on nine tasks.

The paper evaluates more than final policy success. Held-out expert-video VOC measurements, qualitative failed-versus-successful trajectory analyses, component ablations, alternative temporal-modeling designs, and experiments using human videos provide complementary evidence.

The cross-domain experiment is promising: supplementing one in-domain demonstration with 20 fixed- or varying-view human videos improves simulated-policy learning on three tasks, suggesting that heterogeneous passive video can be useful.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The main construction, integration with DrQ-v2, baselines, and qualitative motivation are easy to follow, while curves report means and standard deviations over eight seeds.
The authors acknowledge an important limitation involving tasks with back-and-forth motion rather than presenting temporal position as universally equivalent to task progress.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification does not establish the claims made about the actual method. Equations 8–9 only describe cost-to-go along an assumed optimal expert trajectory. The learned pairwise function F(o_t,o_{t+1}) is not constrained to equal a difference of a scalar potential, to be path independent, or to preserve the optimal policy. Consequently, potential-based shaping theory does not justify the learned reward on exploratory out-of-distribution transitions.

The claimed “suboptimal awareness” is insufficiently supported. Reversing two frames from a successful trajectory supplies examples of backward expert progress, not stalls, failed grasps, off-manifold configurations, or arbitrary unsuccessful behavior. Moreover, the concatenation architecture does not enforce antisymmetry as claimed; it is merely trained on labels having that pattern. Evidence on suboptimality consists primarily of two hand-selected trajectories and downstream results.

The method is not successful as a standalone learned reward under the reported interaction budget. The principal experiments add a privileged binary environment success signal, while Appendix Figure 12 reports zero completed tasks for all methods when that signal is removed. This materially limits the framing that passive video supplies the needed reward and means performance may depend strongly on the unspecified mixing coefficient alpha.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Crucial parameters and procedures are absent, including alpha in Equation 7, lambda in the exponential sampler, frame sampling rate and trajectory lengths, image preprocessing/augmentation, exact broadened Meta-World initialization ranges, success-reward timing, reward normalization or clipping, evaluation and checkpoint-selection protocols, and baseline-specific hyperparameters. The manuscript also provides no usable project URL or code artifact.

The widened initialization distribution is central to both the results and the explanation for poor OT/ADS performance, but it is neither precisely specified nor accompanied by results under the standard benchmark initialization. This makes the fairness and reproducibility of the baseline comparison difficult to assess.

Several conclusions overreach the evidence. All policy learning and evaluation occur in one simulator and task suite; the human videos only augment reward training for three simulated tasks, so the paper does not demonstrate real-world policy learning or broad generalization across embodiments. Temporal distance also conflates elapsed demonstration time with semantic progress and assumes roughly monotone, comparably paced demonstrations.

The empirical results are provided almost entirely as small learning-curve plots without numerical tables, per-task final estimates, aggregate metrics, or uncertainty for method differences. Although eight-seed standard deviations are shown, it is difficult to verify the stated nine-of-ten superiority or judge whether several close differences are statistically meaningful.

The ablations remove components but do not directly validate their proposed mechanisms—for example, measuring temporal prediction calibration, exact antisymmetry, behavior on controlled stalls/regressions, or sensitivity to lambda, bin count, demonstration count, and reward coefficient. Some causal explanations offered for task-specific drops are therefore speculative.

Originality is moderate rather than high: predicting relative temporal position from frame pairs and using it as a reward is a straightforward extension of established temporal representation, ranking, and progress-reward approaches. The paper distinguishes itself mainly through the particular regression/discretization and sampling combination plus strong empirical performance.

The limitations and ethics treatment is too brief. There is no dedicated discussion of human-video participant consent, privacy or data governance, the risk of learning timing and embodiment shortcuts, reward hacking, safety when deploying learned rewards on physical robots, or compute costs. The single sentence about back-and-forth motion does not cover the method’s main assumptions and failure modes.

strengths: Soundness: The main simulation study is reasonably broad, covering ten Meta-World tasks, eight random seeds, several relevant imitation-from-observation and progress-reward baselines, held-out-video evaluation, and component ablations.

Significance: Learning dense feedback from action-free videos addresses an important bottleneck in robotic reinforcement learning. Combining human videos with limited in-domain data is a potentially useful direction.

Originality: Directly predicting signed, normalized frame-to-frame temporal distance, together with short-interval sampling and two-hot discretization, is a simple and practically interesting combination.

Presentation: The method and experimental questions are organized clearly, figures are generally readable, and the appendix honestly reports the important negative result that proxy rewards alone achieve no task successes.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central justification is substantially overstated. Reversing the order of two expert frames does not simulate stalls, failed grasps, loops, or other out-of-distribution failures; both frames remain on the expert manifold. Consequently, the training objective provides no demonstrated reason that arbitrary suboptimal transitions should receive negative rewards. Figure 4 examines only two hand-selected failures and cannot establish this broad claim.

Soundness: The learned pairwise score is not constrained to equal the difference of a scalar potential or to satisfy cycle consistency. Therefore, the potential-based shaping argument in Section 4.3 does not apply to the implemented reward, and an agent may accumulate positive reward through cycles or exploit pairwise inconsistencies. The derivation only describes uniform progress along an optimal demonstration and proves neither policy invariance nor off-demonstration generalization.

Soundness: Appendix A.3.2 reports zero successes on every task when the sparse environment reward is removed. Thus, the impressive main results require an external success oracle, contrary to broad claims that temporal distance itself supplies sufficient task-completion guidance or eliminates manual reward design. The manuscript does not isolate how much performance comes from that oracle, and its weight alpha is not reported.

Evaluation: Evidence is limited to one simulated benchmark, scripted expert demonstrations, and 150k-frame plots despite the abstract's claim about 200,000 interactions. There are no real-robot policy experiments, statistical significance analyses, numerical result tables, robustness tests for distractors or variable execution speed, systematic reward-hacking tests, or evaluation on tasks with non-monotonic progress.

Evaluation: The cross-domain conclusion is too strong. It covers only three Meta-World tasks, always retains one in-domain demonstration, and evaluates policies only in simulation. The study lacks matched-data controls that would distinguish useful human semantics from regularization or increased video diversity, so it does not establish generalization to new domains or embodiments.

Reproducibility: The project-page entry is empty, no code or data release is identified, and essential details are missing: alpha, temporal-sampling lambda, video lengths and frame rates, image preprocessing and augmentation, reward normalization, success termination, evaluation protocol, and baseline-specific hyperparameters. The expanded Meta-World initialization ranges are also unspecified, although they materially affect several baselines.

Originality and significance: Temporal position/distance supervision and progress-based video rewards are closely related to TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, and PROGRESSOR. The paper's principal additions are mostly training-design choices, while the claimed qualitative advance—reliable suboptimality awareness without online refinement—is not convincingly established.

Presentation and limitations: Several claims use unsupported language such as 'causally grounded,' 'exactly' quantifying progress, and treating the environment reward as an upper bound. The brief limitations paragraph mentions only back-and-forth motion, omitting dependence on expert timing, success labels, possible cyclic reward exploitation, simulation-only evidence, and shortcut learning.

Ethics: The work appears low risk, but the manuscript gives no information about consent, participant handling, or release conditions for the newly collected human videos. This should be documented, especially if the videos or identifiable imagery will be released.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical study is substantial: ten Meta-World tasks, eight-seed learning curves, held-out demonstrations, multiple relevant reward-learning and imitation-from-observation baselines, privileged BC/dense-reward references, and controlled component ablations. Significance: Learning useful dense rewards from action-free video addresses an important bottleneck in robotic RL. A frozen reward model that can outperform prior learned rewards—and often the benchmark's engineered dense reward—is potentially valuable.

Originality: Predicting signed, normalized temporal distance between arbitrary frame pairs is a simple and appealing formulation. Combining reverse-order pairs, short-interval-biased sampling, and two-hot prediction produces a method meaningfully distinct from frame-goal value estimation and binary rank prediction, even though the individual ingredients are familiar.

The ablations support the practical importance of signed pairs, weighted sampling, discretization, and pairwise rather than single-frame modeling. The held-out value-order evaluation also provides useful evidence that the model is not merely memorizing training trajectories.

The human-video experiment is promising: supplementing one simulator demonstration with 20 human videos improves downstream simulated-policy learning under both fixed- and varying-view conditions, suggesting that cross-embodiment video can contribute useful supervision.
Presentation is generally clear and well organized, with an intuitive method, helpful diagrams, a broad related-work discussion, and hyperparameter tables for the reward model and DrQ-v2.
weaknesses: The central explanation for out-of-distribution robustness is not fully supported. Reversing two frames from a successful expert trajectory supplies negative temporal direction, but does not simulate failed grasps, stalls, off-manifold states, or other suboptimal behavior as claimed. Evidence on failures consists primarily of two selected trajectory visualizations; a systematic quantitative evaluation on held-out failed and adversarial trajectories is needed.

The theoretical section is only a motivation along optimal expert trajectories. It does not establish that the learned pairwise predictor is a potential difference, is cycle-consistent, preserves the optimal policy, or generalizes to agent-generated observations. Because the deployed reward is an unconstrained adjacent-frame score, cyclic reward accumulation and reward hacking remain possible.

The strongest RL results still use an external binary success signal. In the proxy-only appendix experiment, no method, including TimeRewarder, achieves a success within 200,000 frames. This materially narrows claims about eliminating manual reward design and should be emphasized in the main paper.

The evaluation remains limited to ten tasks from one simulated benchmark. Human videos are used to improve a simulator-trained agent, but there is no real-robot policy evaluation. The cross-domain study covers only three tasks and does not isolate whether gains arise from human-domain content, increased data volume, or regularization; matched-size and shuffled/mismatched-video controls would strengthen the conclusion.

Statistical reporting is incomplete despite using eight seeds: most results appear only as dense learning-curve figures, without exact final scores, confidence intervals, aggregate metrics, or statistical tests. The paper also does not clearly report whether reward-model training and baseline tuning were independently repeated across seeds.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for a convincing acceptance-level result. Important details such as the success-reward coefficient alpha, exponential-sampling coefficient lambda, observation resolution and frame rate, demonstration lengths, image augmentations, reward normalization, baseline-specific hyperparameters, evaluation protocol, compute requirements, and model-selection procedure are absent. The displayed project-page field is blank and no code or data release is identified.

Limitations are treated too briefly. Beyond back-and-forth tasks, the paper should discuss dependence on demonstration speed and pauses, multiple valid task orderings, visually aliased progress, non-expert videos, reward exploitation, and the required success detector. The newly collected human-video dataset also lacks a statement about participant consent, privacy, and intended release or licensing. These are low-risk concerns here but should be documented.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, practically useful approach: signed frame-pair temporal-distance prediction, weighted toward local pairs and discretized with two-hot targets, yields a dense visual reward without expert actions or manually engineered dense rewards. The manuscript is clearly motivated and generally well organized. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/b2a1b6d44a8741fa9fdc5037230a6613/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for this setting: ten Meta-World tasks, eight-seed RL curves, eight primary baselines, additional OT variants, privileged BC/environment-reward references, a ManiSkill task, and component/design ablations. TimeRewarder achieves the strongest final performance and sample efficiency on 9/10 primary tasks.

The evaluation investigates more than downstream success: held-out value-order correlation, successful-versus-failed trajectory reward profiles, backbone and pretraining controls, reward-scale sensitivity, discretization sensitivity, and proxy-only training provide useful diagnostic evidence.

The paper explicitly identifies partial observability and repeated visually indistinguishable states as limitations of single-frame temporal progress. The deterministic fully observable analysis clearly exposes the assumptions under which temporal distance corresponds to progress rather than presenting the connection as universally valid.

The contribution is moderately original and significant. Pairwise temporal supervision is established, but combining signed bidirectional distance prediction, short-interval sampling, and two-hot estimation into an effective observation-only reward is a useful contribution, especially given the strong empirical results and limited cross-domain human-video experiment.
weaknesses: The theoretical result does not justify the central empirical generalization claim. It establishes a time-to-go relationship only along an optimal trajectory in a deterministic, fully observable MDP. It neither shows that a model trained exclusively on successful expert frames assigns appropriate rewards to off-manifold RL transitions nor covers stochasticity, variable execution speed, nonoptimal demonstrations, or visual aliasing—the conditions that matter in the experiments.

Reverse-ordered expert pairs are described as implicit negative examples that simulate failures, but they contain only successful, on-manifold frames. Moreover, concatenation does not architecturally enforce antisymmetry. The claim that this construction naturally provides suboptimality awareness is therefore stronger than the methodology supports; the two selected failure trajectories in Figure 4 are illustrative rather than a systematic OOD evaluation.

Successful policy learning still relies on an environment-provided binary success reward. When that signal is removed, no method, including TimeRewarder, completes a task within 200,000 frames. This materially narrows claims that passive video alone supplies an effective reward or removes reward specification: the evidence supports useful reward shaping in combination with a success detector, not standalone reward recovery.

The principal comparison to Meta-World dense rewards is not fully conclusive. The methods have different reward scales, alpha is calibrated using the first 100 online trajectories, and the paper does not provide matched reward normalization or tuning details for the environment-reward reference and baselines. Numerical tables, confidence intervals, and statistical tests are also absent, making several graph-based claims—particularly sample-efficiency advantages—hard to assess precisely.

Figure 5 analyzes a feature-difference variant rather than the default concatenation architecture used for the main results. Consequently, its attractive representation geometry is not evidence about the actual evaluated TimeRewarder model, despite being used to explain that model's robustness.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives core TimeRewarder and DrQ-v2 hyperparameters, but omits code/data availability, software versions, compute budget, exact image preprocessing and augmentation, full baseline-specific settings and tuning budgets, exact broadened initialization ranges, pair-selection details after sampling a temporal gap, and sufficiently precise collection/preprocessing details for the human videos.

The cross-domain evidence is promising but limited to three visually corresponding tabletop tasks and requires one in-domain Meta-World trajectory; human-only training performs poorly. Thus, broad claims about generalization across domains, embodiments, and diverse in-the-wild video sources should be tempered.

The impact discussion is too cursory. Human-video consent and data governance are not described, and relevant deployment risks—reward hacking, unsafe robot exploration under erroneous visual rewards, and failure under perceptual aliasing—are omitted. These are not fatal ethical concerns for the simulation-focused study, but they should be addressed before real-world use.

strengths: The method is simple and computationally practical: it learns a task-specific dense signal from action-free demonstrations using normalized temporal-distance labels, weighted pair sampling, and two-hot discretization.

The empirical study is broad within Meta-World: ten tasks, eight seeds, several relevant reward-learning and imitation-from-observation baselines, shared DrQ-v2 policy learning, backbone controls, and component ablations. The reported downstream gains are large on most tasks.

The paper includes useful diagnostics beyond final success, including held-out temporal-order correlation, successful-versus-failed rollout traces, representation visualizations, reward-only experiments, and an additional ManiSkill task.
The human-video experiment is a promising indication that heterogeneous demonstrations can help when only one in-domain video is available.
Presentation is generally clear and the authors explicitly acknowledge perceptual aliasing and back-and-forth trajectories as limitations.
weaknesses: The central justification for generalization to suboptimal behavior is unsound. Reversing the order of two frames from a successful trajectory does not generate suboptimal observations or out-of-distribution failures; it only supplies an opposite label for the same expert frames. Consequently, claims that this construction naturally recognizes stalls, loops, failed grasps, and other unseen behavior are not established.

The theory proves only that time-to-go is related to value along an optimal trajectory in a deterministic, fully observed MDP. It does not justify the deployed reward model under partial observability or distribution shift. Moreover, the unconstrained concatenation network is not forced to be antisymmetric, additive, or representable as a difference of state potentials, so the claimed connection to potential-based shaping and resistance to reward hacking does not follow.

The strongest qualitative claims—such as temporally coherent and causally grounded feedback—are inferred from selected trajectories on only two tasks. There is no systematic evaluation on failed or adversarial rollouts, no measurement of reward-model calibration off the expert distribution, and no test for exploitable reward cycles.

All successful main experiments retain an environment-provided binary success detector. When that signal is removed, no method, including TimeRewarder, completes any task within the evaluation budget. This substantially narrows the claim of learning rewards from passive video and makes the assumption that success labels are easily available through humans or VLMs important but insufficiently evaluated.

The cross-domain evidence is limited to three simulated target tasks and lacks comparisons with cross-domain baselines. Human-only training fails, while mixing human videos with one in-domain video helps, but the paper does not isolate whether this reflects meaningful embodiment transfer, generic visual augmentation, or experimental tuning. There is no real-robot policy evaluation.

Exact quantitative comparison is difficult because most results are shown only as learning curves without tables of final performance, confidence intervals, aggregate metrics, or statistical tests. Some broad statements, including outperforming the environment reward on nine tasks, are therefore hard to audit precisely.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims: no code or data availability statement is provided, and important details such as image preprocessing, augmentations, demonstration lengths, widened initialization ranges, camera configuration, RL update/evaluation schedules, baseline-specific hyperparameters, and the human-video collection protocol are missing. The adaptive success-reward coefficient also depends on the first 100 rollout trajectories, introducing implementation-sensitive and potentially method-dependent scaling.

The limitations and ethics treatment is incomplete. The impact statement is largely boilerplate and does not discuss consent or privacy for the collected human videos, failure of learned rewards under distribution shift, reward hacking, or safety implications of deploying such rewards on physical robots. Overall, the idea and results have merit, but the unsupported generalization mechanism and insufficiently reproducible evidence require substantial revision before others can reliably build on the work.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical study is broad and generally well controlled: ten Meta-World tasks, eight seeds, a common DrQ-v2 learner, shared CLIP-ViT backbones for key baselines, held-out-video evaluation, component ablations, and additional ManiSkill and proxy-only experiments.

Significance: Dense reward construction from action-free videos addresses an important bottleneck in visual robotic RL. The strong sample-efficiency gains over several progress-based and imitation-from-observation baselines make the approach practically interesting.

Originality: Signed frame-wise temporal-distance prediction is a simple but useful refinement over temporal ordering, goal-conditioned value learning, and three-frame relative-progress estimation. Weighted short-interval sampling and two-hot prediction form a coherent design for step-level feedback.

Presentation: The method and motivation are easy to follow, and the qualitative reward curves, representation visualization, and extensive appendix help explain the observed behavior rather than reporting only final success rates.

The authors appropriately acknowledge the single-frame method's failure under visual aliasing and back-and-forth motions. This honest limitation, together with the suggested history-conditioned extension, improves the paper.
weaknesses: The central framing is overstated: successful downstream learning depends strongly on an environmental binary success reward. Appendix A.4.5 reports zero completed tasks within the budget when that signal is removed. Thus the demonstrated method is effective reward shaping from videos plus task-specific success detection, not a standalone replacement for engineered or annotated rewards as parts of the paper imply.

Normalized temporal separation is only an indirect proxy for semantic progress and conflates progress with demonstration speed and trajectory length. Reverse-ordering frames from successful trajectories does not actually simulate stalls, failed grasps, or other off-demonstration behavior. The claim of suboptimality awareness is therefore stronger than the supervision warrants and is supported mainly by two selected qualitative failures plus downstream performance.

The theoretical section establishes only that time-to-go is monotonic along an optimal trajectory in a deterministic, fully observed setting. It does not justify generalization of the learned pairwise predictor to policy-generated observations, robustness to different execution speeds, or policy invariance of the resulting approximate reward. The manuscript acknowledges perceptual aliasing but not these broader gaps.

The evidence remains predominantly simulation-based. The real-world human videos are used only to improve reward learning for simulated control on three tasks; there is no real-robot policy evaluation. The cross-domain comparison also confounds domain diversity with additional data volume, so it does not isolate why human videos help.

Several strong conclusions rely on small plots without numerical result tables, confidence intervals, significance tests, or a stated number of evaluation episodes. In particular, the claim of outperforming privileged environment rewards would benefit from tabulated final performance and area-under-curve comparisons, as well as investigation of whether the short training budget disadvantages those rewards.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Core hyperparameters are listed, but code and data availability are not stated, and important details are missing for demonstration preprocessing, image resolution and augmentation, evaluation protocol, baseline-specific tuning, reward scaling, checkpoint selection, and the exact construction and licensing of the human-video dataset.

The impact statement is generic. Although the immediate ethical risk is limited, the paper should document participant consent and privacy handling for the collected human videos and discuss safety risks from deploying learned, potentially hackable visual rewards on physical robots.
